title: On Doctors, Mechanics, and Computer Specialists: The Economics of Credence Goods
pub: Journal of Economic Literature, vol. 44, no. 1, pp. 5-42
author: Uwe Dulleck · Rudolf Kerschbamer

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source analyses fraud and efficiency in credence-goods markets, not legal AI capability or work redesign. Its treatment of verifiability, liability and institutional conditions may offer an analogy for AI governance, but it does not provide enough evidence to accept, extend or reject the cluster’s proposition.

st.t: Credence incentives: More information may not improve service
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s incentive-and-accountability framing and materially develops it by specifying when verifiability or liability, commitment, customer homogeneity and price design can induce honest provision. It also shows that removing these conditions can produce rationing, overcharging, duplicated diagnosis costs or market collapse, supporting the cluster’s rejection of information alone as a universal remedy.
qs: We have shown that ineﬃcient rationing and ineﬃcient treatment of some consumer groups may arise if condition (i) fails to hold, that equilibria in- volving overcharging of customers or specialization of experts - both leading to a duplication of search and diagnosis costs - may result if condition (ii) is violated, and that the credence goods market may break down altogether if condition (iii) doesn’t hold.

st.t: Expert matching: Observable work may remain unsuitable
st.an: The source accepts that expert-service quality cannot be reduced to observable delivery and materially develops the proposition by distinguishing undertreatment from overcharging and specifying when liability or verifiability can induce efficiency. Its benchmark gives pricing a stronger theoretical role than the cluster’s empirical evidence does, but only under restrictive assumptions that the source itself treats as limited.
qs: The key feature of credence goods is that consumers do not know which quality of a good or service they need.

st.t: Service necessity: Verifiability cannot ensure proper treatment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core distinction between verifying delivered treatment and determining whether that treatment was necessary. It also supplies the restrictive theoretical benchmark under which verifiability and incentive-compatible pricing can produce honesty, while acknowledging strong assumptions and practical gaps rather than treating verifiability as a generally sufficient safeguard.

kp.k: Credence goods involve uncertainty about necessary treatment
kp.d: Dulleck and Kerschbamer develop a theoretical framework for expert services, including medical treatment, repairs and computer sales, rather than discussing AI or legal services directly. Experts can diagnose needs that consumers cannot identify themselves. Successful treatment need not reveal whether the intervention was necessary, and consumers may also be unable to establish what was actually provided.
qs: The key feature of credence goods is that consumers do not know which quality of a good or service they need.
Furthermore, he may not even be able to observe whether a suggested treatment quality was actually provided or not.

kp.k: Undertreatment, overtreatment and overcharging are distinct problems
kp.d: Undertreatment supplies insufficient quality and sacrifices potential benefits; overtreatment incurs additional costs without commensurate benefits. Overcharging means billing for a more expensive intervention than was delivered. The authors distinguish inefficient treatment from transfers between consumers and experts, while noting that overcharging can eventually discourage beneficial consumption.
qs: The additional benefits to the consumer from the sophisticated intervention are less than the additional costs.

In the long run such overcharging also leads to an ineﬃciency if consumers postpone car repairs or medical check-ups and the like, because of the high prices they have paid for these services in the past.

kp.k: Prior empirical studies motivate the incentive problem
kp.d: The article reports evidence from earlier studies, not new empirical research: Emons (1997) cites a Swiss study finding that an average person's probability of receiving one of seven major surgical interventions is one third above that of a physician or physician's family member. Wolinsky (1993, 1995) cites a Department of Transportation survey estimating that more than half of auto repairs are unnecessary. The authors also report that Gruber et al. (1999) find cesarean delivery frequencies respond to insurance fee differentials, and Hughes and Yule (1992) associate cervical cytology treatment volumes with fees.
qs: Wolinsky (1993, 1995) refers to a survey conducted by the Department of Transporta- tion estimating that more than half of auto repairs are unnecessary.
As the evidence cited above reveals, these diﬀerences in abilities aﬀect the treatment prescribed in medical environments.

kp.k: Market efficiency depends on specific institutional conditions
kp.d: The central theoretical result is conditional: markets resolve the fraudulent-expert problem without efficiency loss when consumers are homogeneous, consumers are committed to treatment after diagnosis, and either delivered treatment is verifiable or liability prevents insufficient treatment. Large economies of scope between diagnosis and treatment motivate the commitment assumption. This is a model result, not an empirical finding that real expert markets generally function efficiently.
qs: Proposition 1 Under Assumptions H (Homogeneity), C (Commitment), and either L (Liability) or V (Verifiability) or both, market institutions solve the fraudulent expert problem at no cost.
This no-fraud result suggests that asymmetric information alone cannot explain experts’ cheating.

kp.k: Verifiable treatment supports honest equal-margin pricing
kp.d: With homogeneous consumers, commitment and verifiable treatment, but without liability, equal absolute markups across interventions remove incentives to choose the wrong treatment. Consumers infer incentives from posted prices. A monopolist captures the surplus; unconstrained Bertrand competitors price at treatment cost. The result also depends on the commonly known assumption that indifferent experts choose appropriate treatment. Verifiability here means the ability to observe and prove delivered treatment, not checking AI output.
qs: Consumers infer the experts’ incentives from the intervention prices.
Consequently, the best they can do is to post equal mark-up tariﬀs and to behave honestly.

By assumption, an expert provides the appropriate treatment if she is indiﬀerent between providing the appropriate and providing the wrong treatment, and this fact is common knowledge among all players.

kp.k: Liability can support fixed-price efficient treatment
kp.d: When liability prevents undertreatment but delivered treatment is not verifiable, the model predicts efficient treatment at a constant charged price. Experts minimize costs by supplying the cheapest sufficient intervention; consumers anticipate that differing posted prices would lead to charging the higher price. Monopoly pricing extracts consumers' available surplus, whereas competition produces a price equal to expected treatment cost. The authors discuss HMOs as an illustration but later qualify this analogy because effective liability is difficult to secure.
qs: Under the liability assumption ex- perts charge a uniform price for both types of treatment and serve customers honestly as the following result shows.
Consumers know this and expect the expert to charge the higher price and then to provide the cheapest suﬃcient treatment.

kp.k: Combined safeguards leave only overtreatment incentives
kp.d: When both liability and verifiability apply, liability rules out undertreatment and verifiability rules out overcharging. Efficient provision then requires the expensive treatment's markup to be no greater than the cheap treatment's markup. Equal markups are therefore sufficient but not necessary in this case.
qs: There remains the incentive to provide a major treatment when the consumer only needs the minor one.
This overtreatment incentive disappears if prices are such that the mark-up for the minor treatment exceeds that of the major treatment.

kp.k: Heterogeneity enables exclusion and discriminatory treatment quality
kp.d: With heterogeneous consumers and expert market power, a single tariff can exclude high-expected-cost consumers even when treating them would be efficient. Allowing multiple tariffs enables discrimination through advice quality: in the examined case, low-expected-cost consumers receive serious diagnosis and appropriate treatment, while high-expected-cost consumers purchase major interventions and may be overtreated. The authors report that heterogeneity in valuations can instead generate undertreatment. These inefficiencies disappear under their unconstrained price-competition assumptions.
qs: As our next result shows, the monopolist uses the quality of advice oﬀered as a self selection device.
When price discrimination is possible, the expert finds it optimal to provide high quality diagnosis and appropriate treatment to low-cost consumers only.
High-cost consumers are potentially overtreated; that is, they are induced to demand a high quality intervention without an honest diagnosis.

kp.k: Second opinions can generate costly market specialization
kp.d: Without consumer commitment, with liability but no treatment verifiability, low diagnosis costs can undermine fixed-price cross-subsidies. Providers specializing in minor interventions attract cheaper cases; consumers with major problems must then visit another expert. The specialization equilibrium requires sufficient competition—at least four experts in the stated lemma—and generates duplicated search and diagnosis costs. These outcomes are conditional, rather than a general claim that second opinions are undesirable.
qs: A constant price across treatments implies that consumers with minor problems subsidize those with major ones.
Specialization is ineﬃcient because it implies a duplication of search and diagnosis costs.
The point is that verifiability allows experts to set treatment prices close to marginal cost. With prices close to marginal cost consumers have no incentive to search for a second opinion.

kp.k: Price restrictions help sustain modeled overcharging equilibria
kp.d: In the noncommitment setting, the authors construct an equilibrium in which experts sometimes recommend expensive treatment unnecessarily and consumers sometimes reject that recommendation and seek another diagnosis. Supporting this particular equilibrium requires restrictions on expensive-treatment prices. With fully flexible prices, a deviating provider can undercut competitors by credibly specializing in minor interventions. The authors use this distinction to qualify earlier models of fraud.
qs: To get the overcharging result studied in the literature, firms’ price setting power needs to be restricted.
Part (ii) of the lemma shows that the overcharging equilibrium ceases to exist if prices are fully flexible.

kp.k: Absent safeguards, undertreatment can collapse the market
kp.d: When neither liability nor treatment verifiability holds, experts always provide the cheap treatment and charge the highest applicable price. Consumers anticipate this. If the expected benefit of cheap treatment covers its cost and diagnosis, trade survives with undertreatment of major problems; otherwise no trade occurs. This result assumes consumers can verify that some treatment occurred. If even that is unverifiable, experts supply nothing and the market collapses regardless of consumer valuation.
qs: Then there is no perfect Bayesian equilibrium in which experts serve customers eﬃciently.
Proposition 4 relies on the assumption that consumers are able to verify whether some kind of treatment has been provided or not.
If this is not the case, each expert always has an incentive to provide no treatment at all and the credence goods market ceases to exist for any value of v (see also the next footnote).

kp.k: Real-world liability and verifiability are imperfect
kp.d: The authors caution that their institutional assumptions are demanding. Repair failures can arise later for reasons unrelated to expert conduct; extended warranties can weaken consumers' maintenance incentives. Returned parts only establish treatment if customers can identify them and their origin. Medical outcomes may be stochastic or difficult to prove in court, making unsuccessful treatment an unreliable indicator of undertreatment. Consumer expertise and economies of scope also vary across settings.
qs: However, some of our organizing assumptions sound more innocent than they really are.
With many sicknesses there is no suﬃcient treatment, with others success is only random.
Thus, a failing treatment is no perfect signal of undertreat- ment.
The existing literature has ignored consumers’ heterogeneity in expertise so far.

kp.k: Insurance creates additional patient and provider incentives
kp.d: The discussion identifies mechanisms beyond the formal model: insurance may reduce self-care incentives and patients' concern about overtreatment because they do not bear full social costs. Patients may seek treatments with positive side effects, while negative side effects can restore incentives for restraint. The authors also raise the possibility of insurer–physician collusion to undertreat expensive cases when it cannot be proven; this is a proposed incentive mechanism, not an established empirical finding.
qs: On the one hand, patients have less incentive to properly take care of themselves because health risks are covered by insurance.
On the other hand, they are less worried about overtreatment as they do not carry the full social costs.
All these indirect incentive eﬀects are not addressed in our model.

kp.k: Model limitations constrain real-world pricing conclusions
kp.d: The authors explicitly acknowledge restrictive assumptions, including binary problems and treatments, observable treatment costs, take-it-or-leave-it prices and perfect diagnosis. They also identify a tension between efficient equal-margin pricing and consumers' willingness to pay: with idle capacity, equal absolute margins on a fuse and an engine may be unacceptable to consumers. With tight capacity, equal profit per unit of capacity is the relevant condition. The paper presents its framework as a benchmark requiring further robustness work.
qs: It rests on the assumption that there are only two possible types of problem, that only two types of treatment exist, that treatment costs are observable, that posted prices are take-it-or-leave-it prices, that experts can diagnose a prob- lem perfectly, and so on.
By contrast, if experts hold idle capacities then the absolute mark-up has to be the same for both types of treatment.
But, are consumers really prepared to pay the same absolute mark-up for a fuse as for an engine?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Dulleck and Kerschbamer make conditional claims about expert-service markets, not about AI or legal-service transformation.
pts.d: In this cross-domain source, the authors model credence goods: services where experts can identify customers' needs better than customers themselves. They claim that market pricing can eliminate fraudulent treatment under specific conditions. With verifiable treatment, equal treatment mark-ups can induce appropriate provision; with liability but unverifiable treatment, a uniform price can induce efficient treatment. Relaxing their assumptions can produce exclusion from service, inappropriate treatment, overcharging, duplicated diagnosis costs, or market breakdown. These are theoretical equilibrium results rather than forecasts of technological change.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The central evidence basis is a unifying formal model and comparison with existing theoretical literature; cited empirical studies and market practices motivate and illustrate the analysis.
pts.d: The authors derive propositions and lemmas using game-theoretic equilibrium analysis. They reproduce or qualify results from prior credence-goods models rather than conducting a new empirical study. Motivating evidence includes previously published findings about surgical interventions, unnecessary repairs, and responses of medical treatment to financial incentives. Their discussions of repair pricing, computer sellers, insurance brokers, travel agents, taxis and HMOs are illustrative interpretations, not direct empirical tests of their propositions. The cited empirical results belong to the referenced researchers, not to new data collected by Dulleck and Kerschbamer.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims have no forecast horizon and depend on restrictive informational, contractual and market assumptions.
pts.d: The supplied text identifies an August 2005 version of a paper published in 2006. Its results concern equilibrium conditions, not dated predictions. The efficiency result requires homogeneous customers, commitment after diagnosis, and either enforceable liability against insufficient treatment or verifiability of treatment supplied. Verifiability here means customers can observe and prove the delivered treatment, not human checking of AI output. Further modeling assumptions include known treatment costs, perfect expert diagnosis, posted take-it-or-leave-it prices and honest treatment when experts are indifferent. Heterogeneity-related inefficiencies require market power. Without commitment, low costs of obtaining another diagnosis can support inefficient specialization; the particular overcharging equilibrium also requires restrictions on price flexibility. Without both liability and verifiability, experts provide only cheap treatment, and trade disappears when customers' expected benefit is too low. The authors explicitly qualify the realism of their assumptions and acknowledge a mismatch between some model predictions and common experience.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are expert suppliers and their customers, particularly in repair, medical care, taxi services and computer retail.
pts.d: Customers can receive insufficient or unnecessarily costly treatment, pay for treatment not delivered, incur repeated consultation costs, or be priced out of beneficial service. Under the authors' price-discrimination model, customers with a higher expected cost of treatment can receive unnecessarily sophisticated interventions, while lower-cost customers receive appropriate diagnosis and treatment. Under their ideal efficiency conditions, a monopoly expert captures the surplus, whereas price competition transfers it to consumers. Technical knowledge can help customers establish what was supplied; less knowledgeable customers may have fewer protections. Medical patients face particular difficulties because outcomes may be uncertain and treatment quality hard to establish. The source does not identify AI-specific winners or losers or make claims about lawyers' employment.
